conventions.convention: Inner products are linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second; this fixes the shape of Cauchy-Schwarz, of the adjoint pairing, of Riesz representation and of every scalar measure E_{x,y}(B) = ⟨E(B)x,y⟩.

A Hilbert basis (orthonormal basis) is a complete orthonormal family; the index set is arbitrary, no countability or ordering is assumed, and vector expansions are norm limits over the net of finite subsets.
Sums over an arbitrary index set are finite-subset suprema (square-summable families); this is the reading of Bessel, Parseval and of the Hilbert-Schmidt square-sum s_E(T).
T is compact when the image of every bounded set has compact closure; the closed unit ball suffices, and compactness implies boundedness rather than assuming it.

Hilbert-Schmidt is defined only relative to a supplied Hilbert basis E, via s_E(T) = sup over finite F of Σ_{e∈F}‖Te‖²; basis-independence of the property and of the norm is a theorem, not part of the definition.

The spectrum is defined by failure of invertibility: λ ∈ ρ(T) exactly when λI − T is bijective with bounded inverse; the operator spectrum is compared with the spectrum in C*(I,T) only through spectral permanence.

A projection valued measure is strongly countably additive (norm-convergent series of projection values), with E(∅) = 0, E(X) = I and E(B∩C) = E(B)E(C); weak additivity is shown equivalent to strong additivity, and regularity means each scalar measure E_x = ⟨E(·)x,x⟩ is a regular Borel measure.

The PVM integral of a simple function is read off a disjoint normal form covering all of X, with a zero-coefficient complement allowed and no empty presentation; representation independence is proved before the symbol is used.
Complex L² spaces consist of a.e. classes with ⟨f,g⟩ = ∫ f ḡ (linear in the first variable); this is the pairing used by kernel operators.

The torus is T = R/Z with the quotient topology, compact and homeomorphic to the Euclidean circle, and its normalized Haar integral is defined on the fundamental domain [0,1); abstract Haar theory is deliberately not invoked.

Choice strength is declared per item: AC_ω for sequence-level results, DC where countable recursion is used, and full AC from the Gelfand/spectral-construction items onward; DC is proved to imply AC_ω.

Standing nonzero-space hypothesis: when a statement needs H ≠ {0} it says so (bounded Borel PVM integral, spectral theorem, Borel calculus), while the zero space is handled separately where needed (Hilbert-Schmidt definition, classification theorem).

The spectral PVM of a normal operator is the unique regular PVM on the Borel σ-algebra of σ(T) with ∫ z dE = T; uniqueness is part of the spectral theorem and the Borel calculus is defined through this E.

load_bearing.statement: Real or complex inner-product space: the pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and ‖v‖ always denotes the induced length.
In an inner-product space |⟨u,v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖ ‖v‖ for all u, v.
A Hilbert space is an inner-product space complete for the induced norm.
For a closed subspace M of a Hilbert space, H = M ⊕ M^⊥, and x − P_Mx ∈ M^⊥ characterizes the orthogonal projection P_M.
Assume AC_ω. Every bounded linear functional f on a real or complex Hilbert space H is f(x) = ⟨x,y⟩ for a unique y ∈ H, with ‖f‖ = ‖y‖, and y depends conjugate-linearly on f.
A Hilbert basis (orthonormal basis) of H is a complete orthonormal family, i.e. one whose closed linear span is H; no enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part of the definition.

Assume AC_ω. For an orthonormal family in a Hilbert space the following are equivalent: completeness, zero complement, Parseval's identity Σ_i|⟨x,e_i⟩|² = ‖x‖², and convergence of the finite-subset net P_Fx → x.

Assume AC_ω. For a complete orthonormal family (e_i) in a Hilbert space, x is the norm limit of the finite-subset net Σ_{i∈F}⟨x,e_i⟩e_i, the coefficients are unique, and the expansion is unconditional (support at most countable).
T : X → Y is compact when for every bounded A ⊆ X the closure of T(A) is compact in Y; equivalently when the closure of T of the closed unit ball is compact, and then T is bounded.
Assume AC_ω. If X is normed, Y Banach, each T_n : X → Y compact and ‖T_n − T‖ → 0 for a bounded T, then T is compact.

If ‖R‖ < 1 then I − R is invertible with inverse the norm limit of Σ_{n<N}R^n and norm at most (1−‖R‖)^{-1}; if A is invertible and ‖A^{-1}E‖ < 1 then A + E is invertible with (A+E)^{-1} = (I + A^{-1}E)^{-1}A^{-1}.

T is Fredholm when ker T is finite dimensional, ran T is closed, and coker T = Y/ran T is finite dimensional; then ind T := dim ker T − dim coker T ∈ Z. The range's closedness is an explicit hypothesis and no index property is asserted here.
Assume AC. If T : X → Y and U : Y → Z are Fredholm between Banach spaces, then UT is Fredholm and ind(UT) = ind U + ind T.

Relative to a supplied Hilbert basis E, s_E(T) = sup over finite F ⊆ E of Σ_{e∈F}‖Te‖²; T is Hilbert-Schmidt relative to E when this is finite and then ‖T‖_{HS,E} = s_E(T)^{1/2}. The basis is part of the notation and no basis-existence claim is made.

Assume AC_ω. s_E(T) = s_{E'}(T) for all Hilbert bases E, E' of H and s_E(T) = s_F(T*) for every Hilbert basis F of K; membership and the Hilbert-Schmidt norm are therefore basis-independent, and when the common sum is +∞ no HS norm is defined for any basis.

Assume AC_ω. If T is Hilbert-Schmidt relative to a Hilbert basis E of H, with P_F the coordinate projections, then TP_F is compact and ‖T − TP_F‖ ≤ (Σ_{e∈E\F}‖Te‖²)^{1/2} for finite F; consequently T is compact.

Assume AC. For σ-finite (X,μ), (Y,ν) and k ∈ L² of the completed product, the section integral defines a bounded T_k with ‖T_k‖ ≤ ‖k‖₂, and for every Hilbert basis E, F one has Σ_E‖T_ke‖² = Σ_F‖T_k*f‖² = ‖k‖₂², so T_k is Hilbert-Schmidt with ‖T_k‖_HS = ‖k‖₂.

Assume AC. For a bounded normal T on a nonzero complex Hilbert space there is a unique isometric unital star-isomorphism C(σ(T)) → C*(I,T) with z ↦ T (and f ↦ f(T)), where σ(T) is the nonempty compact operator spectrum.

A PVM on a measurable space is a map B ↦ E(B) into orthogonal projections with E(∅) = 0, E(X) = I, E(B∩C) = E(B)E(C), and norm-convergent strong countable additivity; it is regular when X is locally compact Hausdorff and every E_x(B) = ⟨E(B)x,x⟩ is a regular Borel measure.

Assume AC_ω, H nonzero. For bounded measurable f there is a unique Φ_E(f) with ⟨Φ_E(f)x,y⟩ = ∫ f dE_{x,y}, obtained as the norm limit of uniform simple approximations; moreover ‖Φ_E(f)‖ = ‖f‖_{E,∞}, ⟨Φ_E(f)x,x⟩ = ∫ f dE_x and ‖Φ_E(f)x‖² = ∫ |f|² dE_x.

Assume AC. Every bounded normal T on a nonzero complex Hilbert space has a unique regular PVM E on the Borel σ-algebra of σ(T) with ∫ z dE = T and Φ_E(f) = f(T) for continuous f; conversely the coordinate integral of any regular PVM on a nonempty compact Λ is bounded normal with spectrum inside Λ and norm at most max|z|.

concerns.concern: The closing 'Sharpness remark' asserts W(M_t) = (0,1) for multiplication by the coordinate on L²(0,1) and itself says 'no item of this pair proves it in detail'; only the two inclusions are sketched (pointwise bounds for unit vectors, interval indicators for the reverse). The claim is true, but it is carried as informal commentary inside a theorem item and is not a proved statement of the library.

Well-definedness clause (7) asserts that the measure class of μ and the a.e. class of the multiplicity function are independent of the chosen cyclic decomposition 'by the intertwiner lemma and the classification theorem proved immediately below on this page'. The definition therefore defers its own invariance to items that take this definition as input; there is no circularity in the mathematics, but the definition is not self-contained and a reader must read forward to justify the notation.

Clause 1 states 'E(U) ≠ 0 for every nonempty relatively open U ⊆ σ(T); equivalently the support of E is σ(T)', but no support is defined for a projection valued measure anywhere in the PVM definition on this page; the operative content is the displayed condition on relatively open sets, and 'support of E' is used as an informal synonym.
